headline: Texas and derailment accidents lead 197,608 reports from 1975 to 2026. Rear end collision (Accident type) is up 129.4% in the last 12 months (13 vs about 5.7 expected).

metrics.label: Accidents analyzed
metrics.explanation: Reports left after removing duplicates and rows with no date or state.

metrics.label: Top state
metrics.explanation: The state with the most reported accidents, and its share of all reports.

metrics.label: Top accident type
metrics.explanation: The most common kind of accident in the reports.

metrics.label: Top equipment type
metrics.explanation: The kind of train or equipment involved most often, among reports that name one.

metrics.label: Unusual months
metrics.explanation: Months whose count was far from what trend and season predict.

metrics.label: Categories spiking now
metrics.explanation: Types, equipment or causes with a clearly higher last 12 months than before.

findings.statement: Accidents cluster in a few states: the top three hold 24.4% of reports.
findings.evidence: Texas leads with 19,067 reports. The top county is Cook, IL with 8,801.
findings.so_what: Focus inspections and safety reviews on the leading states and counties first.

findings.statement: Derailment is the most common accident type.
findings.so_what: Match safety rules and training to the accident types that happen most often.

findings.statement: Freight Train is involved most often among reports that name equipment.
findings.evidence: It appears in 52.64% of all reports (104,016).
findings.so_what: Check whether this equipment simply runs the most, then target its maintenance rules.

findings.statement: One cause stands out above the rest.
findings.evidence: 'T110' is the leading recorded cause (6.14% of reports, 12,137).
findings.so_what: Put prevention effort behind the leading causes before smaller ones.

findings.statement: 48 months were unusual compared with the normal pattern.
findings.evidence: The largest outlier is October 1976, a spike with 1049 reports against about 846.7 expected.
findings.so_what: Look into what happened in flagged months, such as weather, events or reporting changes.

method_notes.why: Group-and-count tables answer which causes, places and equipment appear most.
method_notes.alternative: A regression model could weigh factors together, but counts are easier to explain and enough here.

method_notes.why: Counting by state and county shows where accidents cluster on a map.
method_notes.alternative: Exact coordinates would allow finer clusters, but this data only gives state and county.

method_notes.why: STL removes trend and yearly season, so only truly odd months are flagged.
method_notes.alternative: A simple average and standard deviation is easier, but trends and seasons would cause false alarms.

method_notes.why: Comparing the last 12 months with the prior 3 years shows which categories are rising.
method_notes.alternative: A full forecast model could be used, but it needs more tuning and is harder to explain.

caveats: Counts are raw totals. They are not adjusted for how many trains or miles each state or railroad runs.
Reporting rules and dollar thresholds can change over time, which can move counts without any real change in safety.
The most recent months may be incomplete because reports arrive late.
Missing equipment, cause or county values were labeled 'Not recorded' and are left out of the leading-category findings.
County names repeat across states, so counties are always paired with their state.
The cause column used was 'Primary Accident Cause Code'.
Accidents here are those reported on Form 54 and do not cover every incident type, such as some crossing events.
